@pjamiesonkay Good 

And I’m clarifying that it could impact more than just private equity and insurance companies

I think that’s part of it. But for many physicians, the bigger issue is cash flow.

An insurance-based practice can mean waiting 60, 90, even 120 days for meaningful revenue. Meanwhile, rent, payroll, malpractice insurance, EMR costs, billing infrastructure, and your own bills don’t wait.

And if you’re running a procedure-based practice or an office-based business, the upfront costs can be even higher. You may need to purchase equipment, supplies, technology, and other infrastructure before you’ve generated meaningful revenue.

Even a bare-bones practice needs enough capital to keep the doors open while you’re waiting to get paid. Once you add the infrastructure and equipment required to actually operate the practice, the numbers can go up quickly.

Politicians, Employers,  and insurance companies seem to love capitalism until a physician wants to retain their freedom or negotiate.

If I choose not to join your network, I should be able to negotiate payment for my services. You should not get to impose the terms of a contract I never signed.

You want to sell out of network coverage while controlling what physicians outside your network are paid. All the benefits of a negotiated contract without actually negotiating one.

And then there are all the times those services are reimbursed at zero dollars and zero cents. The physician provides the care, and the insurer pays nothing.

Patients should be protected from surprise bills. Physicians and insurers should resolve payment between themselves.

Stripping physicians of bargaining power is anti capitalist. It concentrates power, undermines independent practices, and risks leaving patients with fewer choices and less access to care.

It is stupid and dangerous policy. Healthcare will suffer for it.

The current rapid drive towards incorporating AI into critical infrastructure without guard rails is dangerous.

AI is a powerful and useful tool, but it does not provide objective advice. It reflects the data, instructions, and incentives of whoever controls it and can be easily manipulated.

In healthcare, an insurer might tune AI toward cost savings over care, a surgical company toward procedures and implants, or a supplement company toward its own products, all while sounding neutral.

All of which have potential for real harm.

The risk is amplified by consolidation. The UK competition regulator identified more than 90 AI partnerships and investments involving the same six major technology companies and warned of dependence on a handful of firms.

This concentration creates systemic risk. A hidden bias, security breach, coordinated failure, or flawed update could spread across institutions before anyone understands what is happening.

Centralized AI systems concentrate risk, suppress independent judgment, and allow one failure to become everyone’s failure.

The danger is not merely that AI can be wrong. It is that AI can be shaped to serve whoever controls it, then deliver that bias at scale while appearing objective. We are building critical infrastructure around systems that may be unable to withstand a major failure.

There has been a lot of criticism of the No Surprises Act IDR process lately.

And as someone who was initially reluctant to utilize it because I didn’t want to limit access, I am now its strongest advocate.

The important thing to understand is that almost none of the criticisms address the more obvious question:

How many opportunities did the insurance company have to resolve the claim before an arbitrator ever made a decision?

The process does not go from a physician submitting a claim directly to arbitration.

The insurer first makes an initial payment or denial.

If the physician believes that payment is inadequate, there is then a mandatory 30 business day open negotiation period specifically intended to allow the parties to agree on a reasonable rate. IDR cannot even be initiated until that period is over. (CMS)

And even after IDR begins, the parties can still resolve the dispute rather than having the arbitrator determine the payment.

So there are multiple opportunities to settle the claim.

The bigger question is:

Are insurers actually using those opportunities to negotiate?

In my experience, overwhelmingly, no.

Most of the time the “open negotiation” period is simply quiet.

Sometimes you receive a response offering a very small additional amount.

Across all the claims I have personally been involved with, I can remember one time where there was what I would consider an actual back and forth negotiation over a reasonable payment.

Apparently that experience is not unique.

CMS has now acknowledged receiving numerous reports that parties were not meaningfully engaging in open negotiation before proceeding to IDR. (CMS)

The problem was significant enough that the federal government changed the process and created a formal response requirement during the negotiation period, specifically to improve communication and encourage meaningful negotiation before arbitration. (CMS)

Think about that.

We created a 30 business day negotiation period.

Insurers have an opportunity to make a reasonable initial payment.

They then have another opportunity to negotiate that payment.

The parties can still resolve the claim after IDR begins.

Yet enormous numbers of disputes still make it all the way to an arbitrator.

And then insurers point to the arbitration results and argue that IDR is the problem.

Maybe arbitration is not the first place we should be looking.

Maybe we should be asking why so many claims ever needed arbitration in the first place.

If insurers do not want physicians using IDR, make a reasonable payment.

If they do not want cases going to arbitration, actually negotiate during the negotiation period.

And if they want independent physicians to stay in network, offer reasonable contracted rates.

Arbitration was supposed to be the last resort when negotiation failed.

But if one side barely participates in the negotiation process, it is pretty disingenuous to blame the arbitrator when the dispute ultimately has to be decided.

What insurers fail to mention…

IDR takes several months and gives insurers multiple opportunities to negotiate with physicians.

Before arbitration, there is a required 30-business-day negotiation period to reach a fair payment.

In my experience, most insurers underpay or refuse to meaningfully negotiate during that process— then complain when they lose in arbitration.

Arbitration isn’t the problem. Insurers underpaying physicians and refusing to negotiate in good faith is.

I’m definitely not against data centers.

But I am against subsidizing their energy demand.

If a data center requires major new generation, transmission, or grid upgrades, those costs should be paid primarily by the companies creating the demand—not spread across everyone else’s electric bill, which is increasingly what utilities are trying to do.

The trade I’m willing to make is simple: allow individuals and businesses to generate more of their own electricity and sell excess power back to the grid at market rates.

That creates new supply, offsets some of the additional demand from data centers, and keeps ordinary ratepayers from being stuck with the bill.

What a tone-deaf LinkedIn post on reference-based pricing by the CMO of Blue Cross Blue Shield of Vermont. 

In a state where BCBS is functionally a monopoly with an HHI north of 8,000, this is not a serious cost-control proposal, it is price setting by a dominant payer that already dictates networks, reimbursement, utilization, and access. 

Site-neutral billing addresses hospital arbitrage. 

What is being argued for here is government-mediated reference-based pricing, which in a monopolistic, heavily regulated market simply entrenches insurer power while further compressing independent physicians and narrowing patient choice. 

Vermont already operates under certificate-of-need barriers, rate regulation, and global budgets, yet access continues to shrink and costs continue to rise because the core problem is insurer market power and administrative bloat. 

The most revealing fact is that this monopoly still loses money. That is not an argument for more price controls. It is proof of structural failure in how healthcare is run in Vermont

When someone from a BUCA argues for government-initiated reference-based pricing, they are arguing for a price cap. It may sound reasonable, but it does not solve the problems insurers created. 

Narrow networks, deliberate capacity constraints, heavy regulatory burden, and prior authorization still limit patient access. 

Reference pricing makes network status irrelevant, strips physicians of leverage, and increases insurer margins without any obligation to improve access or service.

When an administrator or insurance executive uses the phrase ‘covered lives,’ they’re not talking about patients. 

They’re referring to a monetary unit. 

A covered life represents predictable revenue tied to enrollment, attribution, and risk scores. 

It’s discussed the same way any other asset is discussed on a balance sheet. 

Care delivery is an expense. 
The covered life is the government backed asset.
